newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Rotterdam bunker volumes grow after poor September.
newsitem.headline: Rotterdam bunker volumes grow after poor September.

text.p: The Rotterdam bunker market which suffered poor volumes in September has improved steadily during October, despite prices rises to new highs and cheaper product on offer in Singapore, traders say.
One major supplier estimates fuel oil bunker enquiries in Rotterdam in September reached 370,000 tonnes, the lowest level this year.
The average monthly total is about 450,000 tonnes and traders said the October average was heading back to that level.
The first half of October has shown a marked improvement on September's poor performance, suppliers and brokers say.
"In the first half (of September), volumes were particularly bad as people simply asked for emergency quantities, but there has been a gradual improvement since," one broker said.

Some suppliers say shipowners have simply become more accustomed to higher prices and have realised that bunker prices are not about to fall. Bunkers are expensive in line with the worldwide strength of oil prices which jumped at the start of September and have steadily risen since.

Indeed, relative to crude, fuel oil prices are not strong. Rotterdam fuel oil barges are currently trading at about 65 percent of the physical Brent crude price. At the same time last year, fuel oil traded at 70 percent of the crude level.

However, Rotterdam prices have hardly stabilised, climbing to fresh five year highs on Tuesday, when delivered bunkers were at $127 a tonne. Prices have been higher than in Singapore for the past 10 days.
Traders say Rotterdam has probably gained from sharp rises in the U.S. in October. In Houston, bunkers shot up $15 at the start of the month.

Rotterdam also now compares more favourably the rest of Europe. In September, the high prices have proved a minor boon for Europe's second string ports, particularly as maintenance of Rotterdam refineries has left higher quality refinery material in shorter supply and thus more expensive than in certain other European ports.
"We've not drastically reduced the pattern, but to some extent we've moved from Rotterdam to other ports," said a buyer at one shipping line.

On isolated occasions, shippers say they have found that, on occasions, bunkers in Hamburg, Scandinavia in the north and in Fos, Spain and Suez around the Mediterranean have been cheaper than offered in Rotterdam.
On Wednesday, Gothenburg undercut the entire NWE market, providing passing ships with the chance to fill up at bargain prices.
"It could be that they have a requirement to free tank space or that they simply wanted to cash in on profits made to date," said one buyer.

Shippers policy of only buying essential supplies has also meant they need to buy more frequently, which has involved stop-off for refueling outside the major bunkering centres. The volumes of individual deals has not been large, but some second tier ports and terminals have benefitted.
"The gains have been spread quite widely. Nowhere actually made a killing in September, but smaller ports were able to pick up a reasonable number of enquiries," one broker said.
